reason: Exclusive jurisdiction given to the courts of a city that nothing in the deed connects to the lease (premises, parties' offices, place of signing or of payment). Parties cannot confer jurisdiction on a court that has none (A.B.C. Laminart), so the clause shuts out the competent courts: void under s.28(a). A clause elsewhere in the deed naming the home city, or an arbitration clause, does not save it. The Batch reasons' 'unless facts outside the deed' is dropped (Session 2): refer is only for doubt the deed itself raises, as in PO-16 and PO-61. The key had hand off.

reason: Read alone the bar is absolute, because 'may' go to arbitration is not an agreement to arbitrate (Jagdish Chander). But 'may' does not contradict cl. 5A's 'shall', so cl. 5A is the deed's arbitration agreement and the court bar is its ordinary effect, saved by Exception 1 to s.28 (Enercon). The two clauses differ on who appoints the arbitrator, which is for s.11, not whether there is an agreement (Perkins Eastman, CORE). The bar cannot remove the courts' role under ss. 9, 11, 34 and 36 of the 1996 Act, so nothing is actually restricted: degree partial, as for the 'shall arbitrate; no courts' items (BP-2). The key had void; Batch T3 had refer.

reason: Appropriation of the deposit to sums due 'in the opinion of' the Lessor. A clause belongs under s.28 if it deals with who decides a claim, where or by when, even if it is valid; it is out of scope only if it deals with what can be recovered or has nothing to do with claims (Session 2). 'In its opinion' is the wording where one party decides, so s.28 has to be checked, and the clause passes: the opinion is not made final and nothing stops the Lessee suing or arbitrating over a wrongful deduction. Valid, s.28. degree and alternative_forum are left out: no allowed value fits a clause that restricts nothing. The key had hand off, out of scope.

Cl. 2A allows arbitration only 'if both parties so agree at the time the dispute arises', which contradicts cl. 23A's present promise to arbitrate rather than weakening it. The earlier clause usually prevails (Ramkishore Lal), which would make 2A govern and the bar absolute; against that, courts lean towards upholding arbitration. Weighing the two is for a court: hand off, cross-clause as in PO-59. The bar cannot remove the courts' role under ss. 9, 11, 34 and 36 of the 1996 Act. The key had void.
